questions.q: Which sugar gives a NEGATIVE Benedict's test?
questions.explain: In sucrose the anomeric carbons of both glucose and fructose are tied up in the glycosidic bond, so neither unit can open to a free carbonyl. Maltose and the two monosaccharides are reducing sugars and give brick-red Cu₂O.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes Benedict's reagent?
options: A single stable solution of CuSO₄, sodium citrate and Na₂CO₃
Two solutions, A and B, mixed at the time of the test
questions.explain: Benedict's reagent is one deep blue solution; citrate keeps Cu²⁺ dissolved and Na₂CO₃ makes it mildly alkaline. The two-solution tartrate/NaOH reagent is Fehling's, which is the usual trap.

questions.q: Fructose, a ketose, gives a brick-red precipitate with Benedict's solution because:
options: It has a free –CHO group in its ring form
The alkaline reagent converts it through an enediol into aldoses
Fructose is hydrolysed to glucose by Na₂CO₃
questions.explain: The mild alkali of Benedict's reagent isomerises fructose via an enediol into glucose and mannose, which then reduce Cu²⁺ to Cu₂O. For the same reason Benedict's test cannot tell an aldose from a ketose.

questions.q: Which compound gives a red precipitate when heated with Benedict's solution?
questions.explain: HCOOH is on the same positive list as for Fehling's test, along with aliphatic aldehydes, α-hydroxy ketones and reducing sugars. Aromatic aldehydes and simple ketones stay blue, and sucrose reacts only after acid hydrolysis.
